statement: When two React effects in the same component both react to the same state change (one resets/invalidates a cache, another re-fires a request from that cache's current flags), and both effects' dependency arrays change in the SAME render commit, their DECLARATION ORDER decides which runs first — React runs same-commit passive effects top-to-bottom in declaration order. A reset-then-refetch pair must declare the reset effect FIRST; declaring the refetch effect first lets it capture a generation/version number that the reset effect's own bump (running immediately after, in the same commit) then invalidates, discarding the very request it was supposed to protect.
notes: Discovered while building tests/journey-evidence-layout-browser-regression.test.tsx and tests/stage-receipts-drawer-stale-response.test.tsx for components/journey/StageReceiptsDrawer.tsx — NOT reported by the operator; found only because a real behavioral test exercised the actual timing. A 'fetch when the drawer becomes open, from ANY cause' effect was declared BEFORE the existing 'scope changed, reset caches and bump the generation counter' effect. On a scope change, both effects' dependencies change in the same commit; the fetch effect ran first (because it was declared first), captured a generation number, and the scope effect's own unconditional generation bump then ran immediately after — invalidating that very request the instant it started, before it could ever resolve.

The fix reordered the two effects (reset declared first) rather than adding a second generation counter or synchronizing them some other way — the ordering guarantee React already provides was sufficient once the effects were arranged to rely on it correctly.

Generalizes to any pair of effects sharing a mutable ref/counter where one PRODUCES a value the other CONSUMES within the same render pass — the producer must be declared before the consumer, and that dependency should be stated in a comment at both effects, since nothing in the type system enforces it.

occurrences.defect: The fetch-on-open effect, declared before the scope-change effect, captured a generation number for a newly-selected agent's request that the scope-change effect's own generation bump (running next, same commit) then immediately invalidated — the new agent's own request was silently discarded as 'stale', discovered only via a real deferred-promise test.

canaries.assertion: using deferred, manually-resolvable fetch promises, proves a scope switch's own new request resolves and renders correctly even when it starts in the same commit as the scope-change reset.
source-scan confirming the fetch-on-open effect is declared textually AFTER the scope-key effect in StageReceiptsDrawer.tsx.
